title: Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training for Enhancing Cardiac-Vagal Modulation, Aerobic Fitness, and Endurance Performance: A Methodological Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
authors: Manresa-Rocamora A, Sarabia JM, Javaloyes A, Flatt AA, Moya-Ramón M
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
population: Adults in controlled trials of HRV-guided vs predefined endurance training (random-effects SMD)
findings: HRV-guided training was superior for enhancing vagal-related HRV indices (SMD+ = 0.50, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.91) but not resting HR (SMD+ = 0.04, 95% CI -0.34 to 0.43).

Small, non-significant SMDs (p > 0.05) favoured HRV-guided training for maximal aerobic capacity (0.20, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.47), aerobic capacity at second ventilatory threshold (0.26, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.57) and endurance performance (0.20, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.48).
No heterogeneity was found for any aerobic fitness or endurance performance outcome.
Best methodological practice for HRV index selection, recording position, and baseline/daily-change approach (fixed vs rolling averages) requires further study.

Authors conclude HRV-guided training may be more effective for maintaining and improving vagal HRV with less likelihood of negative responses; any superiority for fitness and performance is 'only by a small margin'.
HRV-guided training was superior for vagal-related HRV indices (SMD+ = 0.50, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.91) but not resting HR (SMD+ = 0.04, 95% CI -0.34 to 0.43).

Small, non-significant SMDs favoured HRV-guided training for maximal aerobic capacity (0.20, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.47), aerobic capacity at second ventilatory threshold (0.26, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.57) and endurance performance (0.20, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.48); no heterogeneity for these outcomes.

Authors conclude HRV-guided training may maintain and improve vagal HRV with less likelihood of negative responses, but any superiority for group-level fitness and performance is only by a small margin; HRV index, recording position and baseline method (fixed vs rolling averages) need further study.
limitations: Trial count and total N are not in the abstract; methodological heterogeneity in HRV protocol; confidence intervals include zero for all performance outcomes.
implications: Treat HRV as a tolerance monitor: performance effect is about SMD 0.2 and not significant, so it should not drive large plan changes.

Resting HR did not differ between guided and predefined training (SMD 0.04); this is an outcome comparison, so it argues against giving resting HR its own prescription trigger rather than against using it as a corroborating signal.
Make the HRV baseline method (rolling vs fixed) configurable and label it unresolved rather than presenting one method as proven.

HRV-based readiness adjustment is a justified optional feature but only a minor modifier (e.g. downgrade a hard session to easy after sustained suppression vs a rolling personal baseline), never the planning backbone.
Use a rolling personal baseline (multi-day), not single mornings or population thresholds; the optimal window is not established, so any window length is a default.
Do not promise performance gains; frame changes as lowering the chance of a poor response.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, journal, first author, 29 Sep 2021. All numbers match the Europe PMC abstract (PMID 34639599). Total N not stated so sampleSize null.
